lines: This Roman bridge is almost fifty meters tall. But it wasn't built for people. It was built to carry a river.
The water came from a spring fifty kilometers away. Over that whole distance, the channel could only drop seventeen meters. So every slope was surveyed by hand.
Step one: build the channel. Stone walls, a concrete floor, and a lining of crushed pottery and lime to keep it watertight. Then cover it with slabs.
Step two: when a valley gets in the way, build stone piers, and between them, a wooden frame called centering.
Step three: lift the stones. Blocks of up to six tonnes went up on cranes powered by people walking inside a giant wheel.
The wedge shaped stones lean on each other until the keystone locks the arch. No mortar. Now it holds itself up, and the wood comes out.
Repeat it on three levels, with the water channel on top. Across the whole bridge, it drops just two and a half centimeters.
It carried about forty thousand cubic meters of water a day. And two thousand years later, it's still standing.
